title: The three births — conception, birth, and death as birth (2.1)
hook: the Aitareya counts a person's births, and gets to three, and the third one is what most people would call dying

segments.voice: Yesterday: the self enters through the crown of the head, vidriti. Your line was the door at the top. Did you pause once and ask who was noticing? Day four hundred three.

How many birthdays do you have? One, obviously. It's on your ID. But ask a family and the answer gets fuzzier. There's the day you were born. There's the day, months before, when someone found out you were coming. And in some families, there's a day that comes after the person is gone, when the family gathers and the rites send them on. The Aitareya Upanishad's second chapter counts births too. It doesn't count from the hospital. It counts three, and it puts them somewhere you might not expect.
screen: `HOW MANY BIRTHDAYS DO YOU HAVE?` → `THE DAY SOMEONE FOUND OUT.` → `THE AITAREYA COUNTS THREE.`

segments.voice: The first birth, the text says, happens in the father. The seed is the strength gathered from all his limbs, a self carried in himself. When he places it in the mother, that's the first birth. Then the second. The child becomes one with the mother, like a part of her own body, and so, the text says, she doesn't harm it. She nourishes this self inside her, and so she is to be nourished in turn. The father cares for the child before birth and after, and in caring for the child, the text says, he cares for himself, for so the line goes on and the worlds continue. The child's arrival is the second birth. Then the third. The child grows and takes the parent's place, carrying on the good work. And the parent, having done what there was to do, grows old, and departs. And departing, the text says, he is born again. That's the third birth. Death isn't the opposite of birth here. It's the next one. Then the chapter turns to a seer. It quotes a verse from the Rig Veda in the voice of the sage Vamadeva: while still in the womb, I knew all the births of the gods. A hundred iron fortresses held me down, and like a hawk I broke out. The text says Vamadeva, knowing this, rose up from the body and reached immortality. Notice what the chapter honors along the way. The mother is to be nourished. Even in a list of births, it stops to say who needs care.
screen: `THE FIRST BIRTH: IN THE FATHER.` · `THE SECOND: FROM THE MOTHER.` · `THE THIRD: DEPARTING, BORN AGAIN.` · `VAMADEVA, BREAKING OUT LIKE A HAWK.` · then, large: `THREE BIRTHS.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with the three births. Sit, and think first of the people who carried you before you were born: a mother, a father, whoever held the hope of you. Let one breath be for them. Then think of the day you arrived, the people who fed and held you before you could thank them. Let a breath be for them. Then, gently, think of someone who has died. In the Aitareya's count, that was a birth too. Let a breath go to them, wherever they are. The bell holds the time.

Vamadeva, the seer who said, while still in the womb, I knew all the births of the gods. The Aitareya counts three births: conception in the father, birth from the mother, and death, when a person departs and is born again.
Your line: three births. Today, thank someone who cared for you before you could ask, a parent, a grandparent, anyone who carried you. Day four hundred three.

howItsDone: Hindu life-cycle rites, the samskaras, mark stages from before birth through death, and the funeral rites (antyeshti) and later shraddha offerings are understood by many families as sending the departed on to their next life.

fork.setup: the Aitareya counts three births. the first is in the father, the second from the mother. what is the third?
options: the day you become a parent.
the day you depart this life and are born again.
the day of initiation into study.
fork.reveal: having done what there was to do and grown old, the parent departs, and departing, is born again. the text calls that the third birth.

original.note: Sanskrit Vāmadeva: the Rig Veda seer whose womb verse the Aitareya quotes in 2.5.

trapdoor: what you thought: you're born once and die once.
what it means: the Aitareya counts three births: in the father, from the mother, and in departing, born again.
what a scholar hears: the Vamadeva verse quoted in Aitareya 2.5 is Rig Veda 4.27.1, 'a hundred iron fortresses held me down'.

notes: Aitareya 2.1–4 paraphrased from memory, including 'she doesn't harm it' (na himsati) and 'she is to be nourished' (sa bhavayitri bhavayitavya bhavati). Confirm.
Verse numbering: the Aitareya's second chapter is often printed as one section (2.1) with sub-verses 1–6; the Vamadeva verse is cited as 2.5 here. Confirm.
The text's account is framed around the father; the script keeps that while giving the mother's verse its weight. A Keeper may want to frame this more.
The fork's distractor 'initiation' alludes to the separate idea of the twice-born (upanayana), not taught here.

Editor review (2026-10-01): in 2.3 it is the father (sa) who nourishes the child before and after birth, not 'the parents'; softened 'many families'; the carry's thank-someone action echoes day 390's; left as is because day 404's review picks it up.
